---
title: REST client
---

`ApiClient` is a small `httpx` client for one REST API behind Entra ID. You
subclass it once per API: the class says where the API is and where its
credentials come from, and its methods call `fetch()`.

## A client for one API

```python
from dazapiz import ApiClient


class AppApiClient(ApiClient):
    host_url = "https://app-api.example.com"
    scope = "api://00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000/.default"
    client_id_env = "APP_API_CLIENT_ID"     # this API's service principal
    client_secret_env = "APP_API_SECRET"
    # tenant_id_env = "APP_API_TENANT"      # only if not AZURE_TENANT_ID

    def get_item(self, item_id: str) -> dict:
        return self.fetch("/items/{item_id}", item_id=item_id)


with AppApiClient() as client:
    item = client.get_item("42")
```

`fetch(path, method="GET", *, query, json, headers, content_type, parse,
**path_params)` fills the `{name}` placeholders from keyword arguments,
URL-encoded, sends the request and returns the parsed body: JSON as Python
objects, XML as an `ElementTree.Element`, anything else as text, an empty
body as `None`. A non-2xx response raises `ApiError`, which is also an
`httpx.HTTPStatusError`. `scope` defaults to `f"{host_url}/.default"`, and
`__init__` arguments (`host_url`, `credential`, `scope`, timeouts) override
the class attributes per instance.

## Where the credential comes from

`credential=` wins: any `TokenCredential`, such as `DefaultAzureCredential()`
or `RefreshTokenCredential(refresh_token_from_az_cli())`. Otherwise, when the
class names `client_id_env` and `client_secret_env`, `app_credential()`
chooses one when the client is created, by `mode` (the class attribute),
else `$AZURE_TOKEN_CREDENTIALS`, else automatically:

| Mode | Credential |
| --- | --- |
| automatic | the API's service principal when both of its variables are set, else `"dev"` |
| `"dev"` | `AzureCliCredential`, then `dazapiz.DeviceCodeCredential` in an interactive session |
| `"prod"` | the API's service principal if set, else `WorkloadIdentityCredential` when `$AZURE_FEDERATED_TOKEN_FILE` is set, else `ManagedIdentityCredential` |
| `"client_secret"`, `"workload_identity"`, `"managed_identity"`, `"azure_cli"`, `"device_code"` | that credential alone |

So a developer with neither variable set gets their own `az login`, and a
deployment that sets them gets the service principal. A client ID without
its secret, or the reverse, is a `ValueError` naming the missing variable,
never a silent fall-back. A class with no credential variables and no
`credential=` sends requests unauthenticated.

Tokens are kept until five minutes before they expire. A 401 is not
retried, since the credential would hand back the same token; the token is
dropped so the next request asks for a new one.

## Typed results and model bodies

`parse=` validates the body and types the result:

```python
from pydantic import TypeAdapter

pets = client.fetch("/pets", parse=TypeAdapter(list[Pet]).validate_python)  # list[Pet]
pet = client.fetch("/pets/{pet_id}", parse=Pet.model_validate, pet_id="7")  # Pet
```

`parse` is called with the parsed body of every successful response (`None`
for an empty one). If it raises, `fetch()` raises `ResponseParseError`, with
the method and URL but not the body (a validation error can quote it), and
the original error as `__cause__`. The same error is raised when a body
labelled JSON or XML does not parse.

`json=` takes a pydantic model (sent as
`model_dump(mode="json", by_alias=True, exclude_unset=True)`) or a dataclass,
also nested in lists and dicts. `dazapiz` does not depend on pydantic: any
object with a `model_dump()` method is treated as a model.

## Logging and retries

`verbose=True` logs each call on the `dazapiz.http` logger, in `azr`'s format:

```
ℹ >>> POST https://petstore3.swagger.io/api/v3/pet
ℹ >>> body:
{
  "id": 4711,
  "name": "dazapiz-example",
  "photoUrls": ["https://example.com/dazapiz.png"],
  "tags": [
    {
      "id": 1,
      "name": "dazapiz"
    }
  ],
  "status": "available"
}
✔ <<< status = 200 | time = 0.412 secs. | size = 0.13 Kb
```

JSON bodies (the request's, and the response's on failure) are abbreviated:
an object or array of more than 10 items keeps the first and last 5, an
array of more than 12 numbers or strings the first and last 6, with `...`
between. Headers are never logged, so neither is the bearer token; a secret
you put in a body is logged as sent.

429, 503 and connection failures are retried, up to `max_tries=5` attempts,
waiting for `Retry-After` when the server sends it, else a random 1 to
2.5^attempt seconds (at most 60). A read timeout is not retried: the server
may already have acted.

```
⚠ Request failed. Retrying in 2.1 secs. (attempt 1 of 5).
```

## Example: the Swagger Petstore

`examples/petstore.py` in the repository is a complete, typed client for the
public [Swagger Petstore v3](https://petstore3.swagger.io), with pydantic
models for every body. It needs no Azure, so you can run it:

```sh
uv run python examples/petstore.py
```

The code below is included from that file when the site is built, so it is
the code that runs. These are the choices it makes, and why.

### One base, two kinds of model

<!-- snippet: class _Model(BaseModel): -->
{{< include examples/petstore.py lines="61-81" >}}

- **Aliases.** The API is camelCase (`photoUrls`), Python is snake_case
  (`photo_urls`). `alias_generator=to_camel` maps one to the other, and
  `validate_by_name` with `validate_by_alias` accept either when validating.
  `fetch()` sends models `by_alias=True`, so the wire format is the API's.
- **Frozen.** A validated object cannot be changed behind the validator's
  back; `pet.model_copy(update={"status": "sold"})` makes a changed copy
  (pydantic does not validate `update`, so give it values of the right
  type).
- **Strict requests, tolerant responses.** A request model forbids unknown
  fields, so a typo (`photoUrl=`) fails in Python, before anything is sent.
  A response model ignores fields it does not know, so the server adding one
  does not break the client; a missing required field or a wrong type still
  fails, as `ResponseParseError`.

### Separate input and output models

<!-- snippet: class PetCreate(_Request): -->
{{< include examples/petstore.py lines="98-127" >}}

What you send and what you get back are different contracts. `PetCreate`
checks what the store needs on the way in: a non-empty name and real URLs.
`Pet` always has an `id`, since the store assigned one, and types the photo
URLs as the schema does, as plain strings. Request models are sent with only
the fields you set (`exclude_unset=True`), so an optional field you left out
is not sent as `null`.

### Where the live store differs from its schema

An example client meets the real server, not only its OpenAPI document. The
public store differs in ways the models and methods account for, each noted
in the code:

- The schema leaves a new pet's `id` optional, but the store answers 500 to
  a pet without one: pass your own (as `PetCreate`'s docstring says).
- The store holds pets whose photo URL is the string `"string"`, so `Pet`
  checks the schema's contract (`list[str]`), not a stricter one; only
  `PetCreate` checks for URLs.
- It answers XML unless asked for JSON, so every call sends
  `Accept: application/json`.
- Its `status` query takes one value, so `find_pets_by_status()` makes one
  request per status.
- Its delete reply is plain text labelled as JSON, which would not parse,
  so the delete calls read it as text:

<!-- snippet: # The store labels its plain-text reply ("Pet deleted") as JSON, which would -->
{{< include examples/petstore.py lines="289-293" >}}

### Domain errors

A 404 from `get_pet()` means "no such pet", which callers want to catch by
name, not by status code. The client turns that one case into its own error,
chained to the `ApiError`, and lets every other failure through:
